job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Issue List (as amended Oct. 6) for the Oct. 15 Markup

The five most serious problems are #13, #16, #19, #33, and #22. Any one of them could let mining continue largely unaffected. A summary of priorities is at the end.

### Sec. 2(1): Definition of "commercial deep seabed mining"

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel."** Operators can stay under the 10,000-ton cap by spreading production across several vessels. A fleet of ten ships could legally recover just under 100,000 tons a year.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), tonnage threshold.** Any operation recovering 10,000 tons or less per vessel is lawful, which covers pilot-scale and early commercial mining. The cap also doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry. Freshly recovered nodules hold a lot of water, so this choice changes how much can be mined.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "per year."** The bill doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, a fiscal year, or any rolling 12 months. Operators could time production around the boundary or swap vessels mid-year to reset the count.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" undefined.** The definition only reaches material brought up by a vessel. It may not cover the most damaging activities: running collector vehicles on the seabed, discharging sediment plumes, or dislodging material that is never lifted. It is also unclear who does the "recovering" when a collector, a riser/production vessel, and a transport vessel split the work.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" undefined.** Read literally, this could cover deepwater oil and gas, which is produced at depths over 200 m in volumes far above 10,000 tons. That invites strong industry opposition and conflict with the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. The 1980 Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA) uses "hard mineral resources" and lists nodules, crusts, and sulfides; borrowing that language would be cleaner.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "at depths greater than 200 meters."** The phrase doesn't specify water depth, so it could be read as depth below the seabed. "Seabed" is also undefined, which leaves open whether subsoil deposits are covered.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B), "the Secretary" undefined.** No department is named, so it is unclear whether this means Commerce, Interior, or State. That creates confusion over who can make determinations and gives defendants an easy argument.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B), delegation and vagueness.** An undefined official, using a vague "comparable risks" standard with no rulemaking procedure, decides what counts as a federal crime under Sec. 5(b). This is exposed to vagueness and nondelegation challenges. Courts also no longer defer to agency interpretations after *Loper Bright*.

### Sec. 2(2)–(3): "U.S. person" and "covered vessel"

9. **Sec. 2(2), entity types.** Only "corporation[s]" count. LLCs, partnerships, and LPs are not covered, and most mining ventures and special-purpose vehicles are LLCs.

10. **Sec. 2(2), "a State."** D.C. is not a State, and neither are Puerto Rico or other territories. Entities organized there are excluded, as are federally chartered entities.

11. **Sec. 2(2), foreign subsidiaries.** A U.S. company can mine through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary or a foreign-flagged vessel. Nothing reaches entities owned or controlled by U.S. persons. The definition also leaves out permanent residents and U.S. nationals.

12. **Sec. 2(3), covered vessel.** Vessels under 5,000 gross tons escape registration entirely. "Equipped for the recovery" is vague; for example, a vessel could keep its equipment off board between voyages. The definition is also used only in Sec. 4, so it is disconnected from the "single vessel" standard in the prohibition.

### Sec. 3: Prohibition

13. **Sec. 3(a), "any person in the United States."** The U.S. EEZ and continental shelf are generally not "in the United States." A foreign company on a foreign-flagged vessel could likely mine in U.S. waters. The prohibition should expressly cover the EEZ and the continental shelf.

14. **Sec. 3(a), scope of prohibited conduct.** The bill bans only "engag[ing] in" mining. It does not ban financing, insuring, chartering, processing, or importing deep-sea minerals. U.S. capital and markets could keep funding foreign mining, and the civil penalty has no aiding-and-abetting provision.

15. **Sec. 3(a), no import ban.** Minerals mined by foreign operators can still be sold into U.S. markets. That creates leakage and leaves the economic incentive in place.

16. **Sec. 3(b), grandfather clause.** Any pre-enactment exploration license exempts "mining" with no limit on scale, duration, area, renewal, or transfer. This could permanently exempt the very companies the bill targets.

17. **Sec. 3(b), whose licenses count.** "Exploration license" is not limited to licenses issued under DSHMRA. It may include ISA contracts or licenses from any foreign government. The clause also encourages a rush to obtain licenses before enactment.

18. **Sec. 3(b), exploration versus mining.** The clause lets an exploration license authorize "mining," which is internally contradictory. It invites litigation over whether commercial recovery is allowed.

19. **Sec. 3(c), environmental-assessment exemption.** The exemption has no definition, permit, scale limit, oversight, or time limit, and it turns on the operator's self-declared "purpose." Large-scale "test mining" could proceed indefinitely.

20. **Sec. 3, relationship to DSHMRA.** The bill doesn't repeal or amend DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.). NOAA's authority to issue exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits stays on the books. Courts would have to reconcile two conflicting statutes.

### Sec. 4: Registry

21. **Sec. 4, no penalty.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false certification carries no penalty under this Act. 18 U.S.C. 1001 may cover false statements, but nothing covers non-filing.

22. **Sec. 4, no enforcement machinery.** No agency is given enforcement authority. There is no boarding or inspection power, no vessel-monitoring requirement, no subpoena power, and no vessel forfeiture.

23. **Sec. 4(b), report contents.** The bill doesn't require location, depth, tonnage, or vessel identity. The registry will be weak evidence for enforcing tonnage and depth thresholds.

24. **Sec. 4, jurisdiction and terms.** The section literally applies to every covered vessel worldwide, which is unenforceable for foreign operators and invites extraterritoriality objections. "Operator" is undefined, and there is no deadline to register.

### Sec. 5: Penalties

25. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, effective-date conflict.** Penalties apply from the date of enactment, but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later. Defendants will argue about notice and due process, and courts may resolve the conflict against enforcement.

26. **Sec. 5(a), no procedure.** The bill doesn't say who assesses penalties, whether it happens administratively or in court, or what notice and hearing rights apply. There is also no inflation adjustment.

27. **Sec. 5(b), willfulness only.** There is no lesser "knowing" offense, and "willfully" is a high bar. Because the crime incorporates the vague Sec. 2(1)(B), prosecutions are especially open to challenge.

28. **Sec. 5, no citizen suit, venue, or jurisdiction clause.** Enforcement depends entirely on federal discretion. For conduct on the high seas, jurisdiction and venue are left unclear.

### Sec. 6: International agreement

29. **Sec. 6, "seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months."** It is unclear whether negotiations must begin or conclude within 18 months. Either way, "seek to" is hortatory and unenforceable.

30. **Sec. 6, no accountability.** There is no reporting requirement to Congress and no definition of "equivalent." The bill also doesn't address that the U.S. is not party to UNCLOS or the ISA, which complicates negotiations.

### Sec. 7: Duration

31. **Sec. 7(a), the off-ramp.** "Serious harm" is undefined. Nothing requires or funds the National Academies report. If Congress ever makes the finding, the ban simply ends with no regulatory regime to replace it.

32. **Sec. 7(a), the joint resolution.** A joint resolution is ordinary legislation that Congress could pass anyway, so the clause adds nothing. It may also suggest that a lower burden is acceptable for lifting the ban.

33. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), contradiction.** Subsection (a) says the ban lasts until Congress acts. Subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. Industry only needs to wait out the sunset, and the registry and penalties expire with it.

34. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause.** It is unclear whether violations committed before the sunset can still be prosecuted afterward. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. 109) addresses repeals, so its application to expiration may be litigated.

### Sec. 8 and missing provisions

35. **Sec. 8, 180-day delay.** Operators can mine without limit during the window, which encourages a rush to recover as much as possible.

36. **Missing provisions generally.**
    - No severability clause, which matters given the extraterritorial and delegation provisions.
    - No rulemaking authority.
    - No definition of "person" or "United States." The Dictionary Act likely covers "person."
    - No authorization of appropriations for enforcement.

### Suggested priorities for markup amendments

- Close the EEZ gap (#13).
- Strike or tightly limit the grandfather clause (#16) and the environmental-assessment exemption (#19).
- Remove the sunset or reconcile it with Sec. 7(a) (#33).
- Fix the "single vessel" and tonnage loophole (#1–2).
- Expand "U.S. person" to all entities and controlled foreign affiliates (#9–11).
- Add enforcement authority and registry penalties (#21–22).
- Conform the dates in Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 8 (#25).
- Amend DSHMRA (#20).

This is a policy analysis, not legal advice. I'd recommend having counsel or Senate Legislative Counsel review the priority items before amendment language is finalized. I can draft proposed amendment text for any of these if that would help.
